text: Several B.C. First Nations representing nine communities, together with Cold Lake First Nation in Alberta, have filed judicial review applications in Federal Court to overturn the Pacific Link pipeline’s national‑interest designation, alleging inadequate consultation; the government says it consulted over 110 Indigenous communities and will offer a minimum 10 % ownership interest in the project.

I work as the court reporter, covering everything from lawsuits between squabbling neighbours to murder trials and multi-million judgments in B.C. Supreme Court.
Got my first byline buzz and freelance cheque at age 10 after sending in a one-line \u201cstory\u201d to the Winnipeg Tribune (RIP) for a feature called I Saw That, which invited readers to send in quirks and oddities (in my case, a neighbour who shoveled his walk wearing a Speedo), and I was hooked.
My second newspaper job was delivering the Trib (never got to write for it). Reading the comics in its pages every day engrained a daily newspaper habit, which I still indulge today after the paper lands at my door every morning.
I\u2019m lucky or blessed to have worked doing something I still get a charge out of -- gathering interesting information and sharing it with others \u2014 each new day.

First Nations court challenges pile up against Carney’s Pacific Link pipeline - The Globe and Mail
sources.articleText:
On Oct. 1, Prime Minister Mark Carney declared the Pacific Link pipeline project to be in the national interest. Greg Halinda/The Canadian Press
Indigenous leaders have launched a new volley of court challenges against Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s push to rapidly approve the Pacific Link oil pipeline, arguing Ottawa failed to adequately consult an array of First Nations.
Two new applications for judicial review, representing nine First Nations, call on the Federal Court to quash Ottawa’s declaration of the proposed oil pipeline as a project of national interest.
At a Monday press conference in the Vancouver suburb of Richmond, Indigenous leaders asserted that Ottawa’s plan is unconstitutional and effectively pre-approved the pipeline after cursory talks with some First Nations over three months through the summer.

sources.title: First Nations in B.C. challenge Carney's Pacific Link pipeline 'national interest' designation - CBC
sources.articleText:
Several First Nations in B.C. are challenging the federal government in court and seeking to overturn its decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline project as a project of national interest.
The Pacific Link pipeline, which is planned to transport one million barrels of Canadian crude oil per day, from Bruderheim, Alta., to a deepwater port near Delta, B.C., was designated as a project of national interest in October under the Building Canada Act. That means the federal government has moved from considering whether it should be built to how it will be built by fast-tracking and consolidating the approval process, including environmental assessments.
The nations say listing the pipeline project in such a way "effectively acts as an approval," and that Canada's duties to consult and accommodate the nations must be met before a project is listed.
